scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The loure originated in Normandy, likely during the 16th or 17th century, taking its name from a local bagpipe.
It evolved from a folk dance into a sophisticated theatrical form during the late 17th and early 18th centuries, reaching its height of popularity around 1720.
on_screen: Map: France · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It was not a social dance but a theatrical one, used in operas and ballets to convey dignity, earnestness, and pride.
It was often associated with pastoral scenes or characters of high status.
Today it is a historical tradition.
on_screen: Footage: La Naissance de Vénus (https://archive.org/details/Naissance_de_Venus)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed at a slow or moderate tempo with a noble and majestic character.
It involves two steps per measure, characterized by elegant turns and complex, highly ornamented sequences.
The weight is consistently placed on the first beat, often preceded by an anacrusis.
Watch for Elegant turns.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for the loure is typically in 3/4 or 6/4 meter, featuring a lilting dotted rhythm.
Historically associated with the musette (bagpipe), it evolved into a form for orchestral and solo instrumental performance, often featuring contrapuntal textures.
Listen for the musette (bagpipe), orchestra, harpsichord, violin.
The pulse is 6/4 or 3/4.
A slow, stately sound characterized by a strong, accented downbeat and a lilting, dotted rhythmic pulse that creates a sense of gravity and elegance.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Castor et Pollux — William Christie; Partita No. 3 for violin solo — Hilary Hahn; Orchestral Suites — Jean‐Philippe Rameau, Orchestra of the Eighteenth Century, Frans Brüggen (2008)

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The loure was primarily a theatrical dance performed by virtuosos on the French stage.
It was associated with noble, majestic, and sometimes pastoral settings, requiring costumes suitable for the refined aesthetic of the Baroque court and theater.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Jean-Baptiste Lully, who introduced it to the stage; Raoul-Auger Feuillet, who documented its choreography; and Jean-Philippe Rameau and J.S. Bach, who composed famous examples.
While French in origin, the loure was adopted by German composers like Telemann and Bach, who adapted the form into their own instrumental suites.
The loure is related to the gigue (sometimes called 'gigue lente' or 'gigue lourée') and shares stylistic similarities with the forlane and the bourrée auvergnate.
